title: Form and sound (section 26)
hookLine: those who see me by form or seek me by sound walk the wrong road (as Müller renders the verse)

lines: A FACE, A VOICE, A PHOTO.
cards: Outside a bookstore, a line wraps around the block. A well-known writer is signing tonight. A young man near the front has waited three hours.
He gets his photo, a handshake, the sound of the writer saying his name, and walks away glowing. Then a friend asks what the books are about, and he laughs. He hasn't read them.
He saw the face, heard the voice, and missed the writer completely. Section twenty-six of the Diamond Sutra aims this same mistake at the Buddha himself.

teach.b: The Buddha asks Subhuti whether the Tathagata can be recognized by his bodily marks, the signs tradition says a great being bears. The sutra has asked this before; here it adds a sharp reason for the answer no.
If the marks were enough, a wheel-turning king, a world ruler who bears the same marks, would be a Tathagata too. A body can look the part and not be the thing. Then the verse.

teach.h: NOT BY FORM, NOT BY VOICE.
teach.b: In paraphrase: those who see me by my form, and those who follow me by my voice, have set out on a wrong road. They will not see me. Form is what the eye catches, sound what the ear catches.
Both are real, and both are the outside. The second half of the verse is easy to skip.
The Buddhas are to be seen from the Dharma; their body is the Dharma. And the Dharma's nature isn't something the mind can grab as an object.
So the verse closes one road and points down another: you meet the Tathagata where the teaching is lived, not where the outline of a body stands. What the verse doesn't say matters too.
A Buddhist temple may hold images and chanting.
Read in a room like that, the verse doesn't ask anyone to tear the images down or fall silent.
It asks where the looking stops. A statue can be a doorway. The mistake is to stand in the doorway admiring the frame.

how: Mahayana Buddhists chant and study the Diamond Sutra, and some communities recite its verse on form and sound by heart; it's read alongside the images and chanting of temple life, as a reminder of what they point to.

o: the Tathagata isn't found by his looks or his voice
the five senses a monk learns to switch off
the two gifts a Buddha gives: an image and a chant

games.q: not by form or sound: tap the pairs.
p: bears the marks, yet isn't a Tathagata
where the Buddhas are to be seen

s: the verse tells Buddhists to get rid of statues
it closes a road, not a temple: it asks where the looking stops.
the verse has a second half about seeing from the Dharma
the Buddhas are seen from the Dharma; their body is the Dharma.
the bodily marks prove someone is a Tathagata
the Buddha says a wheel-turning king bears them too.

games.q: you're Subhuti. the Buddha asks: can the Tathagata be recognized by his bodily marks? what does the sutra answer?
o: no: a wheel-turning king has the marks too
only by the marks and the voice together
games.why: the marks aren't enough; then comes the verse: whoever sees him by form or follows him by voice is on a wrong road.

practice: Let your eyes rest on something near you: a photo of someone you love, an image of the Buddha, or just a cup. Take in the form first, the shape, the colors, the edges, and let that be complete.
Then, still looking, ask quietly what it is beyond its shape: the way a person laughs, or the hands that made the cup and the tea it held.

wordCard.voice: Form and sound. The eye's catch and the ear's catch: the verse in section twenty-six says the Tathagata isn't found there, but seen from the Dharma. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit and Pali: form, shape, what the eye sees; the 'form' of the verse in section 26.

carryVoice: Your line: not by form or sound. The face and the voice are only the outside. Until tomorrow.
